result: K27M mutations in H3.1 or H3.3 histone genes are characteristic of pediatric diffuse midline gliomas (DMGs), which are lethal brain tumors.
evaluation: Claims C1, C12, and C13 establish well-documented background knowledge about DMGs and their association with K27M mutations, supported by multiple citations and established in the field.

result: K27M oncohistone mutations dominantly inhibit histone H3K27 trimethylation despite comprising only 5-15% of total H3, through inhibition of the EZH2 methyltransferase.
evaluation: Claims C2, C14, C16-C19 describe the dominant-negative mechanism of K27M mutations, supported by cited literature and experimental data from both Drosophila and human cells (Figures 1A, 1B, 3A).

result: H3K27M oncohistones must be incorporated into chromatin to inhibit H3K27 trimethylation; soluble histone tail constructs lacking the histone fold domain do not inhibit methylation.
evaluation: Claims C9, C37, C49-C51, C53-C54 demonstrate through Drosophila S2 cell experiments that chromatin incorporation is required for inhibition. The histone tail fusion protein experiments (Figure 1A, 1B) provide clear negative controls showing no inhibition without chromatin incorporation.

result: H3K27M oncohistones inhibit H3K27 trimethylation only in proliferating cells; co-expression with the cell cycle inhibitor p21 blocks this inhibition.
evaluation: Claims C10, C30, C36, C59-C64 demonstrate cell cycle dependence through Drosophila eye disc experiments. The p21 co-expression experiments (Figure 2L, 2M) provide clear evidence that cell cycle arrest prevents K27M-mediated inhibition, supported by both cited literature and experimental data.

result: H3.1K27M oncohistone is uniformly distributed across the genome consistent with replication-coupled deposition, showing no enrichment at promoters or active sites.
evaluation: Claims C3, C38, C77, C86-C91, C138 are supported by CUT&RUN profiling data showing uniform genome-wide distribution of H3.1K27M (Figure 3C, 3E) with 4-8 million mapped fragments and no peak formation at promoters or H3K4me2 sites.

result: H3.3K27M oncohistone accumulates primarily at sites of active histone turnover (promoters) with 7,411 distinct peaks, but is also detected at low levels genome-wide consistent with some replication-coupled deposition.
evaluation: Claims C4, C40-C41, C79-C84, C139 are supported by CUT&RUN profiling showing H3.3K27M enrichment at active promoters (Figure 3E), with 44% of peaks overlapping H3K4me2 sites and moderate correlation (R²=0.3) with gene expression. The genome-wide background signal supports dual deposition mechanisms.

result: H3K27 trimethylation is reduced in both H3.1K27M and H3.3K27M cells, but H3.3K27M cells retain some H3K27me3 domains while H3.1K27M cells have dramatically lower levels (2-10% of control).
evaluation: Claims C5-C7, C39, C96, C102, C116-C118, C140 are supported by Western blotting (Figure 3A) and spike-in normalized CUT&RUN data (Figures 3C, 5B) showing quantitative differences between the two oncohistone types. The spike-in normalization validation (Supplementary file 3) strengthens the quantitative comparisons.

result: H3.3K27M cells retain H3K27me3 at a subset of domains: 156 domains shared with wild-type cells (Cluster III) and 1,380 domains absent in wild-type but present in H3.3K27M cells (Cluster IV), while lacking 17,534 domains present in wild-type cells (Clusters I-II).
evaluation: Claims C42, C103-C108 are supported by unsupervised K-means clustering analysis of H3K27me3 domains (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 1). The clustering identifies distinct domain classes with specific gene associations, though the biological significance of Cluster IV domains requires further investigation.

result: Neither H3.1K27M nor H3.3K27M oncohistones interfere with PRC2 binding to chromatin; SUZ12 and MTF2 are present at similar levels in H3K27me3 domains across all cell lines despite reduced methylation in H3.1K27M cells.
evaluation: Claims C8, C43, C126-C134, C141, C144 are supported by CUT&RUN profiling of SUZ12 and MTF2 (Figures 5A, 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and Western blotting (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C). The data show PRC2 components are correctly targeted but activity is inhibited, particularly in H3.1K27M cells.

result: H3.3K27M cells retain active EZH2 enzyme as evidenced by maintained H3K27me3 levels in retained domains, and share epigenomic similarity with embryonic stem cells in lacking most Cluster I and II domains.
evaluation: Claims C109, C114-C115 are supported by the observation that H3K27me3 levels are maintained (not reduced) in retained domains (Figure 4A) and by comparison with H1 ESC and U5 NSC profiles showing similar domain patterns. The inference about EZH2 activity is logical given maintained methylation levels.

result: H3.1K27M-bearing cell lines have biallelic deletions of the CDKN2A tumor suppressor gene, suggesting this secondary mutation is required for cell survival when H3K27me3 is severely depleted.
evaluation: Claims C121-C124 report CDKN2A deletions in H3.1K27M cells (Supplementary file 5) and cite literature showing this is not typical in H3.3K27M cells. However, the causal relationship (C123) is speculative with only two cell lines examined. Additional cell lines and functional validation would strengthen this conclusion.

result: The authors propose a model where H3K27M oncohistones inhibit chromatin-bound PRC2 during DNA replication, with H3.1K27M causing genome-wide inhibition due to uniform deposition while H3.3K27M has weaker effects due to sequestration at active promoters.
evaluation: Claims C11, C44, C145, C148, C153-C156 present a mechanistic model supported by the experimental findings: chromatin incorporation requirement (Figure 1), cell cycle dependence (Figure 2), differential genomic distributions (Figure 3), and PRC2 binding patterns (Figure 5). The model coherently explains the observed differences between oncohistone types.

result: Most DMG patients (~80%) carry H3.3K27M mutations despite only 2 H3.3 genes versus 12 H3.1 genes, and the two oncohistone types are associated with distinct secondary mutations, cancer types, and age of onset.
evaluation: Claims C21-C29 summarize established epidemiological and clinical differences between H3.1K27M and H3.3K27M gliomas from cited literature. These observations motivate the study's investigation of mechanistic differences between the oncohistone types.

result: H3.1 is produced only in S phase and deposited during DNA replication, while H3.3 is produced constitutively and deposited both during replication and at sites of active turnover; these properties are evolutionarily conserved between humans and Drosophila.
evaluation: Claims C31-C35, C45-C48, C55 describe established knowledge about histone biology supported by cited literature. This conservation justifies the use of Drosophila as a model system and provides the mechanistic basis for interpreting the differential oncohistone distributions.

result: H3.3K27M gliomas have increased frequency of ATRX mutations, which may enhance replication-coupled deposition of H3.3K27M and increase inhibitory effects on H3K27 trimethylation.
evaluation: Claims C160-C163 cite literature showing ATRX mutation association with H3.3K27M gliomas and ATRX's role in replication-independent histone deposition. However, the proposed mechanism (C163) that ATRX mutations enhance replication-coupled H3.3K27M deposition is speculative and not directly tested in this study.

result: CUT&RUN profiling with a K27M-specific antibody successfully maps oncohistone distribution in patient-derived DMG cell lines, showing specificity for K27M-bearing cells and detecting both H3.1K27M and H3.3K27M.
evaluation: Claims C65-C70, C73-C76 describe the CUT&RUN methodology and validation. Western blotting (Figure 3A) confirms K27M presence in mutant lines and absence in wild-type controls. Capillary electrophoresis (Figure 3B) shows nucleosomal fragments released only from K27M-bearing cells, demonstrating specificity.

result: Spike-in normalization using Drosophila S2 cells enables quantitative comparison of H3K27me3 levels between samples, validated by linear relationship between read counts and spike-in ratios.
evaluation: Claims C97-C100 describe the spike-in normalization method. The validation experiment (Supplementary file 3) demonstrates linearity, supporting the quantitative comparisons made throughout the study. This methodological approach is critical for the quantitative differences reported between H3.1K27M and H3.3K27M cells.

result: EZH2 automethylation is required for full catalytic activity, and H3K27M blocks this automethylation, potentially contributing to the dominant-negative effect.
evaluation: Claims C146-C147 cite recent literature describing EZH2 automethylation and its inhibition by H3K27M. While not directly tested in this study, this mechanism is presented as a possible explanation for the observed dominant inhibition and is supported by cited work.

result: S phase is critical for maintaining epigenomic patterns through establishment of histone modifications on newly assembled nucleosomes, and H3K27M oncohistones inhibit H3K27 trimethylation only in proliferating cells because EZH2 activity is only needed during replication.
evaluation: Claims C149-C152 integrate cited literature about S phase chromatin maintenance with the experimental observation of cell cycle dependence (Figure 2L, 2M). The logic connecting H3K27me3 stability in non-replicating cells to the requirement for EZH2 activity only in cycling cells is sound.

result: The requirement for different secondary mutations (e.g., CDKN2A deletion in H3.1K27M cells) may explain why H3.1K27M mutations are rarer than H3.3K27M, and suggests the two oncohistone types may confer distinct therapeutic sensitivities.
evaluation: Claims C164-C166 present speculative explanations for clinical observations. While the logic is reasonable given the data, these are hypotheses requiring validation through additional patient samples, functional studies, and therapeutic testing. The therapeutic implications (C166) are particularly speculative.
